Vyāsa said: / “Lord, this burning of Tripura has been heard by me, / wondrous in meaning, just as it occurred. Who could narrate it in such a way?
Why did Guha, becoming enraged, split that Krauñca, the king of mountains? / And why did Vāsava sever the wings of all the monarchs of mountains?”

7.18.m:
Sanatkumāra said: / “Listen, O Vyāsa of great intellect, to what you ask me: / how Mount Krauñca, son of Maināka, was split by Kumāra.
Then Vāsava, having approached Mount Meru, the king of mountains and the abode of all gods, / beheld Skanda as if a mass of fires.
Seeing Kumāra in a grove of reeds, shining like fire, / Śakra, overwhelmed with pride in his sovereignty over the gods, questioned the six-faced one:
‘Who are you, a child of divine form dwelling on Mount Meru, / that seeing me, the king of gods, arrived here, you do not worship me?’
To Śakra speaking thus, the son of the spear-wielder said: / ‘Brahmā and the others know me, as do the Siddhas and those who know the Vedas.
What need is there of knowing me or being worshipped by you, O Śakra, / whose kingdom, gained by austerity, will before long come to an end?’
Then Śakra spoke again to that divine son of Fire: / ‘None is superior to me, except Śarva and the Grandfather.
How can you speak thus to the sovereign of the gods who has arrived? / If you consider yourself greater than me, sinless one—
this is Krauñca, son of Maināka, frequented by Siddhas, / a vast great mountain flowing with many torrents.
Come, come, make a quick pradakṣiṇa [around it] along with me. / Whichever one of us traverses it first—

he shall be the greater of us two through his might and fiery energy.’ / Saying, ‘So be it,’ Kumāra, the six-faced one, then,
having joined with Śakra, mounted on the excellent peacock, / went ahead of Mahendra and circumambulated Krauñca.
Then Mahendra, realising that he was inferior to the son of Fire, / wishing to deceive Kumāra, made a circumambulation only in his mind, / and remained quite at ease, seated on a stone slab.
Then Kumāra, swiftly circumambulating that Krauñca, / quickly spoke upon seeing Indra, ‘I am the victor!’ / ‘I alone am the victor!’ Śakra said to Guha.
As they were speaking thus repeatedly, Śakra and Kumāra, / Krauñca, that earth-dweller, approached and said words: ‘What is this?’
Then Śakra addressed this speech to Kumāra at that time: / ‘This Krauñca of great strength is the witness of our victory.
For he, the noble grandson of the snow-mountain, will not speak an untruth.’

‘Let him be asked, Śakra; what harm is there?’ said the son of Fire.
Śakra said to him respectfully: ‘O mountain, by whom was the circumambulation performed first? / Speak, for you are our authority.’
Then the mountain Krauñca, confused in mind, having reflected for a long time [said]: / ‘This lord of Śacī made the circumambulation around me here first.’
[…] laughing at the gods, the king of mountains spoke thus. / Then, as that mountain was speaking this untruth,
its peak swiftly fell, as if struck by a thunderbolt.

Seeing the great mountain Himavat grieving over the slaying of his grandson, / the daughter of the mountain grieved, gazing repeatedly at the lord of the gods. // 36
Then, as the blessed wielder of Pināka arrived along with the goddess, / those mighty ones, though deeply scorched by sorrow, made obeisance. // 37

Then all those mountains, the goddess daughter of Himavat, / and Śakra the king of gods, rejoiced and worshiped Guha.
The Blessed One too was delighted and granted boons to his son, / and the leader of the host of Mothers went with Guha and the goddess / to the divine, auspicious peak of Mount Himavat.
And the mountains, Meru, Vindhya, and the others, along with Krauñca, / and Śakra the king of gods, the god, repaired to their own abodes.
Thus it was that Krauñca, who dwelt in the Krauñcasārasa, / was split with the spear by Guha and was afterwards made immortal.
And that cleft made by the spear is still seen in Krauñca, the foremost of mountains, / which became wide and vast, an abode of many deities.

All this marvelous splitting of Krauñca has been recounted to you;
any mortal who hears this is freed from all sins.
Vyāsa said:
O blessed one, how is the Supreme Lord the leader of the Mothers?
And who are these Mothers? Tell this to me who am asking:
How were the hosts of Mothers born, and for what purpose?
Of what prowess and of what power are those hosts that came into being, O Lord?
And what is their support by which those auspicious hosts abide?
By whom were they sustained or produced? I wish to know this.
Sanatkumāra said:
Here I shall relate to you the auspicious origin of the Mothers.
Long ago indeed, the blessed Brahmā, having created these diverse creatures,
the lord of the wise ones, wandered about observing them, O Kāleya.
Once that overseer of creatures, when the evening twilight arrived, / reaching a delightful place on the shore of the eastern ocean, / unweariedly performed his twilight devotion for ten million years.

Having performed his twilight devotion, the god seated upon the lotus seat / pondered: 'This delightful place is pleasing to the sight;
here I shall make a delightful city endowed with all desires.'
Reflecting thus, O Vyāsa, the blessed Lord, creator of all,
built an unsurpassed city in that charming region,
of boundless splendor, with red, dark, and golden stones,
furnished with towers, palaces, and moats,
standing as though on four feet with its crossroads.

Then that blessed god spoke once again:
'Here, the best of the gods always showers a myriad of desired wishes; / therefore people are happy in it.'
Having spoken thus, the blessed Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, / went to his divine assembly hall frequented by many siddhas.
When he had gone, O Vyāsa, that city was occupied / by asuras, called Daityas, who were thorns to all brahmins, / whose leader was Asukrodha, the best of all wielders of weapons, / a slayer of brahmins, a destroyer of sacrifices, O brahmin, a slayer of gods and asuras,
along with Siṃhanāda, Bhīmanāda, Mada, and others.
Then the Daityas, led by Haimakuṇḍa, assembled together, / and staying in that foremost of cities, inflicted multiple harassments.
Hating the world, they slaughtered brahmins by the thousands;
the rites of sacrifice, oblation, and the like were interrupted by those vilest of asuras.

7.18.m:
Then the trident-bearing Lord of the gods of gods
asked those foremost of gods turned into women, "For what purpose have you come?"
Then, gathered together, they first reported the devastation by the demons
to Śambhu, and then their own miserable condition as women.
They said, "May we become men again as we were before."
Then the Lord of gods spoke to the gods who had become women:
"Go, all you gods, having become women, into the presence of the demons.
For those Dānavas, arrogant with strength, are to be slain only by women.
Having produced embodied forms, auspicious Mothers, from yourselves,
you shall afterward become just as you were before, O best of gods."

7.18.m:
Then, having bowed again to the Lord, the deities said this:
"O God, make an embodied woman from your own body as well,
with whom we shall forcefully slay the demons, O Supreme Lord!"
Then the God created an auspicious Mother, the goddess Rudrāṇī,
and, assuming a deformed appearance, created a second Mother as well,
named Bahumāṃsā, who embodies the destruction of the universe.
Then, by the command of the God of gods, Lord Viṣṇu as well
created two Mothers: Vārāhī and Vaiṣṇavī.
Brāhmī emerged from the Grandfather, and Śarvāṇī from Śaṅkara;
Kaumārī from the six-faced [god], and Vaiṣṇavī from Viṣṇu;
Vārāhī the goddess from Mādhava, and Māhendrī from Purandara.

7.18.m:
Consisting of all light, the auspicious foremost of Mothers,
Bahumāṃsā the Great Knowledge, arose from the bull-bannered [god].
And from the bodies of all the deities emerged auspicious Mothers,
bearing their own forms and powers, destroyers of the demons:
Vāyavyā, Vāruṇī, Yāmyā, and Kauberī, full of great might,
as well as Mahākālī, Āgneyī, and thousands of others.
Having gone to that delightful city, the goddesses
slew the demons of terrible prowess in many ways with terrible, frightful roars,
and made that foremost city adorned with gold destitute of demons.
Then, all the demons being slain, the God of gods, Umā's lord,
came to that place, wishing to grant a boon to the Mothers.
Seeing all those demons, enemies of the immortals, slain,
the bull-bannered [god], thoroughly delighted, then granted boons to them:
"You shall be the Mothers of the world, become Mother-goddesses.
Those who shall be your devotees, whether foremost of men

or women, O fortunate ones, no harmful beings shall harm them.
And when dead, they shall become my attendants, free from old age and death.
This place of yours, known as Koṭīvarṣa,
shall become renowned in the world, freeing from all sins.
Since I am indeed your cause, and you were created by me alone,
I shall abide here under the name Hetukeśvara, granting boons.
I will dwell together with you, established as your leader.
And whoever worships you along with me according to rule,
his soul freed from all sins, shall attain the supreme state.
Since the Dānavas were slain with a trident by Bahumāṃsā,
this sacred ford shall become known by the name Śūlakuṇḍa.

7.18.m:
Drinking the water of the Śūla [tīrtha] here and bowing to Bahumāṃsā,
the best of men will become unassailable by all harmful beings.
The lovely Mandākinī river, famous as the Pratikūlā,
flowing with floods of blood, shall belong to you here.
I, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the seers rich in austerity
shall compose divine Mother-tantras, the supreme rite of the Mother-sacrifice,
meritorious rituals by which you will receive worship:
the Brāhma, Svāyambhuva, Kaumāra, and Yāmala;
the Sārasvata, with the Gāndhāra, the Aiśāna, and the Nandiyāmala—
these tantras of yours, as well as thousands of others,
shall exist, by means of which men will worship you with devotion;
and you shall grant boons to men who offer sacrifice."

7.18.m:
"Bestowing celestial perfections, O goddesses, endowed with celestial yoga you shall be. / And the women who shall constantly worship you according to the secret rites,
charming women endowed with celestial valor, shall become mistresses of yoga. / Chagala and Kumbhakarṇa, my two leaders of the gaṇas,
shall stand as your doorkeepers by my command. / This place, Koṭīvarṣa, the best and beloved of the Mothers,
shall be an eminent celestial cremation ground, bringing happiness." / Having thus obtained these boons, the Mothers, the Mothers of the World,
having bowed down to the lord of gods with devotion, rejoiced, [though] severely tormented. / Thenceforth they all, along with the moon-crested [Śiva],
dwelt in Koṭīvarṣa, granting fearlessness to all the worlds. / In this way the blessed god, the leader of the gaṇas of the Mothers,
was Śaṅkara, O Vyāsa, about which you asked me.

7.18.m:
Sanatkumāra said: / How the mountains previously had their wings severed by Śakra, / that I shall tell you, O Vyāsa; listen to it all in full.
Formerly, when Hiraṇyakaśipu, the lord of the Daityas and Dānavas, / had been slain by Viṣṇu of supreme splendor, who had assumed the body of a lion,
his son, the Daitya Prahrāda, became enraged against Viṣṇu. / His father being killed, that glorious sovereign lord of the great Daityas
performed fierce, great austerity for many thousands of years. / Then the four-faced god [Brahmā], pleased, approached that sovereign of the asuras himself
and said with respect, "I am the granter of boons." / Having bowed, Prahlāda, his limbs burning with rage, remembering the murder of his father,
spoke this to Brahmā who had arrived to grant a boon: / "Lord, if you are pleased and have come granting a boon:
Viṣṇu killed my father, the king, through delusion. / Act so that I may kill that Viṣṇu in battle."
Then Brahmā said to him, Prahlāda, the foremost of asuras: / "Viṣṇu is unconquerable in battle, and immune to being killed by gods and asuras,
by the grace of the god of gods, the creator of the world, Umā's lord [Śiva]. / This boon cannot be granted by me to you, O great asura.

Even the perfected sky-dwellers envied the valor, / sacred learning, and modesty of the great-souled Prahrāda.

7.18.m:
Desiring tranquility for the attainment of liberation, the great Daitya renounced worldly life, / understanding that rebirth brings sorrow and that supreme impermanence rules all.
Realizing kingship to be painful, Prahrāda, knower of the highest reality, / consecrated his son Virocana to the kingship of the Daityas.
Making him the king of the Daityas and Dānavas, the lord of the Asuras, / desiring the supreme attainment of liberation, resolved to become a renunciant.

7.18.m:
Then, in order to seek the supreme reality—the unborn, auspicious Śiva beyond the qualities— / he approached as a disciple the sage Āsuri, the direct disciple of the blessed Kapila,
and obtained from him the wisdom of liberation. / Realizing the supreme principle beyond primal matters and modifications,
and the conscious soul, the knower of the field, the experiencer who is detached from experiencing, / knowing the ultimate goal of the wisdom of liberation and mastering the doctrines of Sāṃkhya,
he became a perfected sage, best of munis, named Pañcaśikha. / Attaining supreme yoga, that great sage, a master of Sāṃkhya, / freed from the threefold suffering, attained the imperishable abode.
Thus the glorious, great-souled king of the Daityas, an enemy of the three worlds, / after long hostility with Viṣṇu, the preceptor of the gods, / subsequently became a perfected being, granter of fearlessness to the universe, and attained yoga; / freed at last, he reached the immortal state, the primordial Brahman.
Knowing the soul, detached from the gunas, freed from sorrows and the bondages of worldly existence, / liberated from the obstruction of darkness and delusion, that lord of the Daityas became a master of yoga.
In this manner Purandara cut the wings of all those mountains, / O best of sages, as you had previously asked me."
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-second chapter, entitled "The Severing of the Mountains' Wings" in the story of Prahrāda, in the Skandapurāṇa.

The god of gods said:
"It is even so, O sustainer of the world, O you who are bowed to by gods and asuras! / Ascetic vipras are the foremost; they are weightier even than the gods. // 8
Those creatures which are mine were created first, for I am their source; / the Rudras, the twice-born endowed with great splendour, were created by me long ago. // 9
Having observed my creation, Brahmā too, wishing to create, / created brāhmaṇas of great splendour from his head at the very beginning. // 10
I was their leader then, the foremost of the twice-born; / from then on, all the best of vipras became my companions. // 11

7.18.m:
That Pāśupata observance of mine, which destroys death and rebirth— / other castes do not accomplish it, leaving aside the foremost of brāhmaṇas. // 14
I shall declare the characteristic mark of the twice-born; listen to this: / the rules of purity and straightforwardness, their power, and indeed their rites. // 15
One is a brāhmaṇa by birth; by sacramental rite one is called twice-born; / by learning one attains the status of a vipra; the state of a brāhmaṇa is declared to be threefold. // 16
He who is a vipra by birth and he who has mastered the Veda— / in protecting them and in slaying them, the merit and sin are declared to be equal. // 17
And the vipra who is one by birth, proficient in all the āgamas, / endowed with austerity and purity, is called 'thrice-pure.' // 18
Whoever feeds such a one in an ancestral rite or in a rite for the gods— / that becomes inexhaustible for him through the satiation of that purified one. // 19
The vipra who knows the Veda and is constantly dedicated to the fire-offering— / he too is declared the foremost, O goddess; when honoured, he saves his family. // 20

He who is a brāhmaṇa in every way by mere birth, anywhere— / he too is a teacher of the world, O goddess; honoured, he bestows heaven. // 21
The agnihotra, austerity, sacrifice, purity, straightforwardness, / truth, and dedication to the Veda are declared to be the supreme duty of the twice-born. // 22
A brāhmaṇa does not speak untruth; a twice-born does not kill a living being; / a vipra does not render menial service; a twice-born does not become a committer of sins. // 23
A brāhmaṇa who is an ascetic does not obtain rebirth again. / Having attained the status of a learned brāhmaṇa, what indeed has an embodied soul not attained? // 24
Those eight forms of mine which are known, beginning with the sun and moon— / all of them dwell in a brāhmaṇa enhanced by austerity. // 25

7.18.m:
Supported by the splendour of the twice-born, nectar and cattle / are always produced, O goddess; therefore, the vipras are the foremost of all. // 26
Nothing is impossible for those twice-born of supreme splendour; / angered or pleased, they bestow good and ill. // 27
Those twice-born who are ascetics, proficient in the knowledge of the Vedas— / they are the givers of liberation, gods even unto the gods. // 28
I and the Grandfather are declared to be their two wombs: / they were born from me first, O goddess, and then from the Grandfather. // 29
We two are the causes of the twice-born, and you too, by virtue of being nature. / You are declared to be nature (prakṛti), and I am the supreme person (puruṣa). // 30
Those two who are celebrated as Brahmā and Viṣṇu, consisting of the qualities of rajas and sattva— / from us two those two lords of creatures are born at the time of creation. // 31
I am fire; darkness (tamas) is Viṣṇu; goodness (sattva) resides in Brahmā; / know passion (rajas) to be pervasive in the secondary actions. // 32

7.18.m:
These two, tamas and passion, are known to consist of delusion; / sattva destroys those two, and it is born from fire. // 33
For these great-souled twice-born are known to have the fiery splendor of fire; / they prevail everywhere, and there is no checking them.
Know straightforwardness and equanimity to be the fiery energy in twice-born men; / straightforwardness is indeed superior to being endowed with austerity and learning.
Freedom from deceit destroys sins, while equanimity destroys the bondage of delusion; / both of these, practiced by the twice-born as straightforwardness, destroy [sins and delusion].
Long ago, on the bank of the Bhāgīrathī, there was a twice-born man, supreme knower of dharma, / named Dānaruci, who lived by gleaning ears of grain.
His mind was disciplined through all sciences, he granted safety to all beings, / and together with his wife he was devoted to me, intent upon offerings in the fire.

936 / And after first feeding any guest who had arrived, O goddess, / he would eat at the sixth mealtime; such was his excellent vow.
Now as he lived in this manner, a great amount of time passed; / when a guest arrived, no hesitation arose in him.
Endowed with austerity and purity, the twice-born man, devoted solely to straightforwardness, / became exceedingly radiant in fiery splendor, like the sun and fire.
Pleased with his austerity in this way, Fire experienced the highest satisfaction; / he desired to bestow good upon him, granting the fruits he sought.
Then once, in the course of time, when the sixth mealtime had arrived / on a foul day, cold and thick with frosty clouds, the twice-born wandered about;
afflicted by the fatigue of hunger, he did not see any guest. / When even at day’s end no guest was found by him anywhere,
without consuming anything at all, intent upon fasting, / that foremost twice-born did not give thought to his own distress.

“Come, eat; become my guest, good sir,” he said with respect. / Then the wretched outcaste dog-cooker said to that treasury of austerities:
“I am an outcaste dog-cooker, O best of the twice-born; give food right here / to me, a despised person, just as [one would] to beasts and birds.
I am not worthy to receive consecrated food,” he said. / Knowing through meditation that it was Fire present there who spoke thus,
that tiger among the twice-born, skilled in speech, spoke this: / “I neither revile nor worship caste, O sinless one.
For this Self is all-pervading, stationed in all living beings; / with devotion I worship that Self, the supreme Śiva.
Believing the Supreme Lord, the Puruṣa, to be stationed everywhere, / I hold no contempt for animals, especially not for those like you.
Intent on austerity and purity, believing ‘all is indeed He,’ / I worship without agitation; be free of doubt regarding this.
When the Self is all-pervading in worms, insects, rats, snakes, / outcaste dog-cookers, gods, and twice-born, then how could we have contempt?

Addressed thus by the prince of the twice-born, the outcaste dog-cooker was pleased; / then, desiring to bestow grace upon him, he went to the brahmin’s house.
Then Dānaruci, with a mind purified by devotion, / performed the hospitality properly for him, as for an honored guest.
Having been fed, the Fire manifested in personal form, delighted, / and granted him his desired, unexcelled yogic sovereignty.
Having attained supreme yoga, that best of the twice-born living by gleaning grain / was liberated together with his wife, and attained the immortal state.

7.18.m:
Thus has this māhātmya of the twice-born been told properly,
O daughter of the supreme lord of mountains.
Originating from my creation, those foremost twice-born
truly attained such supreme greatness.
Sanatkumāra said:
Setting forth the māhātmya of the twice-born, such was the auspicious,
sin-destroying dialogue that took place between Pārvatī and the supreme Lord.
[…], O son of Parāśara rich in austerity,
ask with a concentrated mind whatever you consider worth hearing from me.
Thus ends the hundred and seventy-third chapter, entitled “Description of the Māhātmya of the Twice-born,” in the Skandapurāṇa.

7.18.m:
Of what kind is that supreme yoga, the auspicious Pāśupata knowledge,
knowing which the accomplished brahmins may attain the highest liberation?
Having been thus asked by his disciple, the best of sages spoke:
Sanatkumāra said:
Well done, O Vyāsa of great intellect! You desire liberation, my son,
since you ask me about that knowledge, the supreme Māheśvara yoga.
That reality which is proclaimed the essence of all yoga traditions,
endowed with the teachings of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, skilled in all internal knowledge,
even having attained the lordly powers of yoga, they did not reach that reality,
not having understood, O fortunate one, the knowledge taught by Śaṅkara.
As it was told by Tryambaka to those dwellers of heaven,
I shall tell you that ascertainment of reality in brief.
It is impossible to describe it in detail even in hundreds of years;
its steady side, destroying the origin of saṃsāra,
which grants liberation and perfection, I shall declare in brief as the supreme doctrine.
Having bowed to Maheśāna, the Puruṣa, the cause of all beings,

who is beyond Prakṛti, secret, the Person, the supreme Lord,
whom the followers of Sāṃkhya call the twenty-fifth Puruṣa, unborn and all-pervading,
and the followers of Yoga [call] the twenty-sixth, omnipresent, consisting of the three guṇas,
who at the time of creation brought forth the two gods, creators of the entire universe,
940
meditating upon the two great-souled Prajāpatis, Viṣṇu and Pitāmaha [Brahmā],
and having bowed down to that Mahādeva, the three-eyed boon-granting Īśvara,
I shall declare his doctrine, the certainty of the conclusion of yoga.
Know this definition of yoga as it is being spoken by me,
by the practice of which, O great sage, the bonds of the bound souls are severed.
When the mind is firmly established in the Self, the external cessation of conceptual thought occurs,
and there is the unification of the soul with the supreme Īśvara.

7.18.m:
This, O Vyāsa, is called yoga, as proclaimed by Śambhu in the past,
subtle and destroying worldly birth for the surrendered celestials.
When the mind of a person dwelling in the body rests within the Self,
free from discursive thought, directed away from the exterior, subtle, applied through practice,
there is the complete cessation of created things marked by subtle conceptions
such as pleasure and pain, for the practitioner who engages in union.
The supreme lord Maheśvara is that intended goal, the unifier,
since there is then union between Īśvara and the individual self.

Attainment of happiness through oneness, from the application of contemplation […],
[…] of the practitioner who is firmly established,
this perfected result would always arise […].
Now the substratum therein is proclaimed in order:
retraction of the senses, then knowledge, likewise control of breath,
meditation, and concentration—this is declared to be the practice of yoga.
Transcending death, these three operations of fourfold nature
exist, and […] death does not have power, O sage.
For his bodily elements indeed become subdued; of this there is no doubt.
Then that practitioner becomes […] [conqueror of] death […].

7.18.m:
These three [activities] always lead to death, characterized by delusion. / There can be no separation in them, in these activities, each one […].
Ignorance wavers in them, even when operating externally and internally. / The practitioner, engaged in these activities, as well as in those situated in the middle,
[achieves] through power the cessation of the elements, the senses, the mind, time, and the directions. / The directions are indeed ten, the divisions of time are three, [along with] the elements and the range of the senses.
Accompanied by the movement of the mind, characterized by the absence of sense-objects— / this was spoken of as pratyāhāra (withdrawal) in the past by the Lord himself.
Because there is no wandering into other directions, when the mind remains motionless, / the emergence of withdrawal arises once in the emergence of yoga.
Knowledge concerning the three times, and supreme mastery: / these two cannot arise when the mind is wavering; they arise together when it is steadfast.

Because this mind is the entire means for the practice of yoga, / one should therefore make an effort towards the mind's single place [of rest].
Meditation during the restraint of the vital breath is remembered as prāṇāyāma. / For the prāṇa breath alone always acts as the charioteer of the [other] winds.
A yogin should constantly practice the restraint of breath; / by progressive attainment, [holding] the wind in the sphere of […].
One should know the sparking of light to be constantly joined with practice: / twice in the apāna, once in the prāṇa, and in the samāna […]
[…] / […]
This third is the kumbha [retention], which kindles the fire of yoga.
By these [breaths], the subtle path of meditation is caused by the restraint of the breath; / through which the yogin progresses and envelopes the supreme Puruṣa.

7.18.m:
From drawing in [the breath] just once, and from releasing it repeatedly, / this is designated as kumbhaka, from the holding of prāṇāyāma and the rest.
This vital breath (prāṇa) is the wind, the self in the body, the living […] / One should know its two forms: coarse and subtle everywhere.
The subtle form is unmanifest, while the coarse is characterized by shape. / Beginning from the coarse, one should discern the subtle through the practice of meditation.
From the fixation upon the subtle, a radiant light arises, O sage. / But for one meditating on a coarse target, the mind wanders in all directions;
when it arises radiant, he should immediately steady it once more. / On a mountain, on a tree, on the path of the wind, in a chasm, in a row of palaces,
on the ocean, or on the earth, he should practice union of the mind.

attachment to the pleasure of sovereignty, and the arrival of much gold and gems: / one should recognize these intuitive obstacles as arising from sattva.
Those accompanied by arrogance of origin, characterized by deviations from proper conduct— / one should know without doubt these intuitive obstacles to be born of rajas.
Consumption, colic, fever, madness, leprosy, snakebite, and planetary afflictions— / preceded by the rise of torment—these one should designate as tāmasic.
A sage, while practicing, should always quickly observe these intuitive [obstacles] / arising from the three qualities, and should immediately remedy them.
Fixing [the attention] on prāṇa and the other [winds], and indeed withdrawing the mind, / he should completely destroy the obstacles through prāṇāyāma and kumbhaka.
Rajas, sattva, and tamas are the three qualities of primal nature (pradhāna); / they belong to that very Great Lord (Maheśa) as the causes for the union with creatures.
These arise through delusion in yoga for a practitioner who possesses egotism. / When the yogin, free from longing, tranquil, and attentive, exerts himself,
then these intuitive obstacles go to destruction equally. / The emergence of these qualities is therefore the cause of delusion.

7.18.m:
One should know tamas to belong to Rudra, sattva to abide in Brahmā, / and rajas to belong to Viṣṇu; the destroyer of them is Maheśvara.
Knowing Mahādeva to be supreme, the twice-born devoted to the practice of yoga, / freed from the three qualities, attains dissolution in Śaṅkara.
First, one should purify one's own body through the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas); / then, by what is taught in the scriptures, free from merit and demerit,
gradually, in accordance with instruction, one should practice meditation, / having conquered the sense-objects such as sound, which fall within the range of the ear and other senses.

7.18.m:
Impartial towards gods and animals, free from the sense of "mine" in all things, / released from all undertakings, free from merit and sin,
free from duality, in a secluded place, he should practice yoga directed towards Īśvara. / Having abandoned egoism along with rules, having ascertained the Sāṃkhya conclusion,
he should constantly practice in the supreme yoga of Maheśvara. / Eight are the eternal material principles, and sixteen are the modifications;
and the twenty-fifth is Puruṣa, the subject of the Sāṃkhya doctrine. / This indeed is the supreme secret in the ascertainment of the reality of the Sāṃkhyas:
having known the difference between Prakṛti and Puruṣa, one is liberated.
Thus ends the hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, the first on the method of meditation, entitled 'The Description of Pāśupata Yoga', in the Skandapurāṇa.

7.18.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
Yoga and Sāṃkhya are everywhere declared to be twofold knowledge. / There, some are devoted to Sāṃkhya, while others have resorted to the path of Yoga.
The unmanifest and Prakṛti, and likewise the ego-sense: / these are indeed eight material principles, together with the five subtle elements.
Five are called the sense faculties of cognition, and five the sense faculties of action; / the mind and the five gross elements are remembered as the sixteen modifications.
And Puruṣa is the twenty-fifth, free from all undertakings, / eternal, omnipresent, subtle, conscious, devoid of the three guṇas,
pure, stainless, the experiencer, a non-doer, standing like a witness. / Knowing him, they do not enter again into this cage of worldly existence.
These twenty-five principles have been declared by the Sāṃkhya yogins, / knowing which indeed one is freed from rebirth.

7.18.m:
Subtle, unmanifest, an object of enjoyment, delighting in all, mutable, / eternal and unconscious, Prakṛti should be known as fulfilling all desires.
Tamas, sattva, and rajas: these are the three guṇas residing in sensory objects, / by whose absence of deviation indeed all this stands established.
Sattva produces illumination, rajas initiates attachment, / and tamas causes delusion: thus the expansion of the guṇas is described.
Of these, bearing the designation of guṇas and having distinct functions and operations, / their operation is called accomplishing [their goal] through the motive of the purpose of Puruṣa.
The divine is eightfold, while that of animals is remembered as sevenfold, / and the human is of one kind; all of this is composed of the guṇas.
Stupefied, unconscious, elemental, gross or subtle, / formless or endowed with form, everything is said to consist of the three guṇas.
These guṇas of the yogin are proclaimed as causing obstacles to liberation; / for bondage belongs only to one who is attached; one unattached is said to be liberated. / By distinction, the triad of guṇas remains constantly abiding in Prakṛti.
Abiding in the modifications according to division, they have resorted according to nature. / The creation of beings is recited by knowers of Sāṃkhya as threefold:

Sanatkumāra said:
How a living creature is born, how it arrives at detachment, / and how it awakens—that, Vyāsa, I tell you. // 1
Space, wind, fire, earth, and likewise water: / from the aggregation of these in one place, that which is called the body is born. // 2
All bodily humours consist of soma, and food is fourfold. / For embodied beings, the production of bodily humour comes from consuming food. // 3
From bodily humour arises blood; from blood, flesh is stated [to arise]. / Fat arises from flesh; from that the bones are formed. // 4
Marrow is to be known as originating from bone; thence arises semen. / From the union of blood and semen, an embryo is formed in a woman. // 5
From the proper timing of the season, and also through the influence of destiny and karma, / at the end of intercourse between a woman and a man, the two having become one, // 6

Held upright by prāṇa and the others, the body stands like a machine. / When repeatedly abandoned by those winds joined with the individual soul, / it shatters in the course of time like an unbaked pot upon falling. / The five elements, having completely departed from the body, / enter the Self, and the Self quickly enters [them]. / Among the elements, the wind is supreme, and the individual soul is bound to it.

7.18.m:
951 / Wind and fire together constitute the individual soul; the individual soul of living beings is not separate [from them]. / No other form of the individual soul of an embodied being is seen at death.
Beyond the fivefold form is considered the deity, subtler than the subtle. / It does not see, nor smell, nor hear, nor speak;
it does not know, nor does it touch—the individual soul enveloped by the vital breath. / The great wind named prāṇa sustains the individual soul, O twice-born one.
Indeed, it shines and breathes in all embodied beings. / That prāṇa sustains the fire, and it is known as the individual soul.
For fire, supported by the wind, turns into active functions. / That which possesses fire in the body is termed the individual soul.
Dwelling within living beings, it is the cause of initiating actions. / Thus this body consists of the qualities of the five elements.

When its modifications have ceased, one is spoken of as dead. / The elements, senses, mind, individual soul, and sense-objects are in the bondage of passion. / In the pericarp of the heart stands the treasury of splendors, / the all-pervading Self, eternal, free from sense-objects and the like.
That omnipresent [Lord] abides there, knowing whom one is liberated. / Through that perfection of yoga by one who knows the practice of meditation,
by steadying the channel-functions through constant practice of yoga, / illumined by splendors, seen, and freed from modifications,
it is seen, O best of brahmins, and liberation is said to follow from that, / indeed by placing dissolution therein through knowledge of the twenty-sixth [principle].
Residing in all living beings, subtle, and established in one's own body— / that which perfected yogins, freed from bonds, behold,

7.18.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
And the inner self is conscious; the mind is known to be born of intention. / And from the movement of the gross elements, the fire of agitation is called the jīva. // 1
There is no consciousness without a body; and if that [body] does not exist, whence could it come? / Nor is consciousness without a jīva, and that [jīva] is also not without a mind. // 2
The prāṇa is called the jīva; from touch another [function] proceeds. / The mind binds everything; the beginning of action is thus, says the scripture. // 3
For all these, coming together, sustain the embodied being. / He among them whose consciousness is paramount is renowned as conscious. // 4
By means of consciousness, one knows the cause of good and evil. / Having fixed that mind in consciousness, one should be constantly delighting in the self. // 5
Transcending sense objects such as sound, having restrained the senses, / intent on undertaking meditation, that embodied soul would become free from karma. // 6
The senses do not bind the mind situated in the body. / The jīva should be understood as bound by nature, through connection with good and evil. // 7
From the excess of rajas and tamas, the two qualities whose nature is unwholesome, / suffering is born; happiness is born from sattva. // 8
Indeed, from the transformation of happiness arises suffering for embodied beings; / and happiness is born again, O brahmin, from the reverse of suffering. // 9

Even having performed unwholesome deeds, even deeds born of great sins, / the creature intent on meditation swiftly brings them to destruction. // 17
Having reached the total destruction of karma through application to meditation, O great sage, / the yogin remains fearless, endowed with supreme lordship. // 18
Desire and wrath, likewise attachment, malice, and fixed passion— / these are lower states; freed from these, one is liberated. // 19
Pride, hypocrisy, egotism, disputation, arrogance, and envy, / harshness and cruelty—these states are bound up with the warrior [nature]. // 8.177.20
He for whom these bewildering [qualities] do not exist, finds the self, the Lord; / he has transcended interior states of delusion, ever equal in suffering and happiness. // 21

Endowed with freedom from possessiveness and other [virtues], he is recited as a yogin. / Having abandoned sacrificial rites, the Vaiṣṇava binding of delusion, // 22
ever devoted to the inner self, a brahmin should become a seeker of liberation. / Having completely abandoned the three aims of life, he who finds delight in liberation // 23
is to be revered by the gods; he is called a [true] brahmin. / Through meditation, karma—whether evil or good—is exhausted. // 24
With karma exhausted, the yogin then attains that supreme brahman. / The meditative sage who has attained yoga, whatever he wishes to do, // 25
that instantly comes to pass for him, even by being thought of in the mind. / Having seen a yogin, persons are immediately freed from sins; / he who even converses with him also attains an auspicious destination. // 26
Knowing that yoga alone is supreme, the liberator from all unwholesome things, / conscious twice-born [sages], O brahmin, indeed became seekers of liberation. // 27
Those who know meditation, the supreme object of meditation, and the creator, / are freed from the afflicter, the affliction, and the afflicted, from the bondage of suffering. // 28
From abandoning all undertakings, from being devoid of possessiveness and the like, / the doctrines of Sāṃkhya and Yoga are one; the distinction is [only] in the liberation of the principles. // 29

7.18.m: The self (puruṣa) among the foremost of the Sāṃkhyas is proclaimed to be devoid of qualities (nirguṇa); / their departure at the destruction of the body is held to be like the extinguishing of a lamp. / The Lord, free from all, is considered the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) according to yogins; / endowed with supreme sovereignty, the yogins enter into Him. / But he who unites the self by means of those concentrations (dhāraṇās) along with prāṇāyāmas, / attains the supreme sacrifice. / The yogin endowed with non-violence and other virtues, devoid of envy, / who practices meditation, conquers death and rebirth.

7.18.m:
Devoid of qualities, free from egotism, having overcome dualities, unrestrained, / consuming food consisting of sustenance obtained by begging, he is called a seeker of liberation (mumukṣu).
Remaining equanimous in all undertakings, abandoned of all support, / transcending the path of ritual action, he is celebrated as a meditator (dhyānin). / He whose mind is not agitated upon the occurrence of sorrow, O great sage, / nor rejoices in pleasure, is proclaimed a meditator. / The path that bestows the perfection of liberation is declared to be threefold: / the first is spoken of as saṃketana; after that, saṃkathana is remembered; / and the third is saṃsakta. Hear now this distinction among them: / having fashioned a likeness of the All-pervading Lord, endowed with the ten observances,
the sage who worships [Him] in meditation is called saṃketana. / Unattached to the pleasures honored by the Veda, having sattva-born actions, without relatives,

having abandoned them, he should meditate on the Lord; this is called saṃkathana. / Because of the renunciation of all undertakings, practiced by Kapila and others, / the path of saṃkathana is remembered as that which kindles the fire of yoga. / But he who, free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa), sees everything as Brahman alone,
with all actions and conduct dissolved, is called a saṃsakta meditator. / And regarding the rules and non-rules of this threefold path,
the various varieties of practice are now fully proclaimed. / All three of these paths of meditation, O sage, are causes of liberation.
Knowing these correctly, free from possessiveness, resorting to any one of them, / the sage then attains the supreme meditation by which he finds that supreme [reality]. / Hear from me, O Vyāsa of great intellect, all these rules of meditation now being spoken, / which bestow the fruit of yogic sovereignty.

7.18.m: Sanatkumāra said: / Brahman is indicated to be twofold: the perishable and the imperishable. / For by knowing both of these, one is freed from all bonds. / The twenty-fifth principle is the perishable; that is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti). / And the imperishable supreme Brahman is remembered as the twenty-sixth. / Having focused the mind on one point again and again through concentrations (dhāraṇās), / one should hold the breath preceded by sensory withdrawal (pratyāhāra). / One should perform sensory withdrawal for half a muhūrta or even a moment; / the restraint of breath (prāṇāyāma) extends from the base upward for one hundred and thirty [measures]. / Fastening whatever seat has been practiced, such as svastika and the like, / one should practice meditation in a solitary place. / Neither afflicted by hunger, nor overfed, nor endowed with pain from illness, / the wise person who desires meditation of the self should not meditate [under such conditions]. / Then, having made the yoga hand-posture, placing the right hand upon the left, / one should turn slightly downwards, looking at the tip of one's nose. / Not touching teeth with teeth, remembering Brahman as the syllable Oṃ, / free from possessiveness, the wise person should meditate preceded by prāṇāyāma. / Joining the self with the Self, he should draw in all limbs; / devoid of craving and with eyes closed, placing concentration in the heart, / motionless as a stone, the sage should practice meditation. / Concentration (dhāraṇā) is remembered as the steady fixation of the mind in one place. / Thus, for that yogin meditating day after day, O sage, / all modifications born of the guṇas, which are causes of obstacles, are destroyed.

7.18.m:
Through the renunciation of all mental states, he undoubtedly attains liberation. / Having made the mind engaged in withdrawal from all sensory objects, / the one free from dualities then joins [in yoga], practicing the fixation of the mind. / Establishing everything in the mind, he should ascertain the supreme reality. / Then, when through the perfection of yoga he sees while meditating / the eightfold perfection pertaining to sovereignty, he is proclaimed a yogin. / When, united [in yoga], he sees gods such as Brahmā, Soma, and the rest, / this is indeed declared by yogins to be a perfection born of yogic modification.
The yogins attain perfection by the mind, through the ascertainment of the principles of the Sāṃkhya.
There is no distinction among yogas, except for the Māheśvara method. // 17

7.18.m:
For yogins [there is] the perfection of meditation, for followers of Sāṃkhya the ascertainment of the principles;
these two, the meditation and the ascertainment of the true meaning of the principles, are not distinct. // 18
Fallen away from all bondage, free from the fault of attachment,
completely rid of passion, delusion, and the like, he is called liberated. // 19
When, engaged [in yoga], he does not meditate upon nor perceive sense objects such as sound,
then, through the repeated perfection of yoga, he sees that Supreme. // 20
Agitated by the fear of death and rebirth, free from the fault of attachment,
adopting silence in the forest, he should meditate on the imperishable syllable Oṃ. // 21
The vowel that is proclaimed at the beginning of the Veda and established in the Vedānta,
which is beyond that [sound] dissolved in nature—that is taught as the Great. // 22
Threefold in place, threefold in morae, threefold in Brahma, and likewise threefold in syllables;
he who knows it as devoid of morae and endowed with morae is liberated. // 23
Neither fire is there, nor wind, nor moon, nor sun;
they have no power in the Great Lord, the Ruler differentiated threefold. // 24

The syllable Oṃ is declared to be the supreme reality, the self, and brahman
by the knowers of the field through awakening to the self, and by the yogins through insight into the subtle. // 25
Always meditating in this very manner, he should unite the mind in the self;
the yogin attains the Lord, having reached whom he is liberated. // 26

Sanatkumāra said:
That Great [Principle] which was described by me as perfected in the internal organ,
together with the five organs of action and the five organs of cognition, // 1
the five elements, and the mind here—these are taught as sixteen modifications.
The Great [Principle], intellect, ego-sense, and the five subtle elements— // 2
these eight, O Vyāsa, are the primary natures residing in the body.
These twenty-four principles have been declared by yogins;
the body exists pervaded by these, which permeate the three worlds. // 3
In the center of the navel are established one hundred and one channels;
and those other [channels] in all the limbs carry water, food, and fluids. // 4

Thirty thousand of them are situated in the stream of vyāna;
other channels of udāna are established in the crown of the head. // 5
Relying on the hub of the circle, it is established within the aggregate of elements;
and in its center, touched by the guṇas, is the active self, deluder of beings, // 6
resembling the radiance of stars, possessing luster like a mass of moonlight,
causing obstacles to others, standing like ten thousand suns, // 7
arisen like portentous fire, resembling mountain mist,
abiding in the guṇas, the womb of beings—the twenty-fifth, the puruṣa. // 8
Beyond even him is the pure one, risen like a great fire,
radiant, blazing on every side, free from conceptual construction, stainless, // 9
resembling a smokeless ember, whose actions and traditions are incomprehensible,
the twenty-sixth puruṣa, subtle, the supreme Lord, all-pervading. // 10

7.18.m:
This very one, O Vyāsa, is declared to stand beyond the beyond;
having known this Mahādeva, a sage is liberated in that very instant. // 11
Abiding in the transformations of the three guṇas, the twenty-fifth is described;
therefore he transmigrates repeatedly, deluded by ignorance alone. // 12
Deluded by passion, he wanders among gods, humans, and animals;
through absorption in the twenty-sixth, his perfection arises from [transcending] modification. // 13
Freed from action and effect, all-knowing, creator of all, sovereign,
filled with supreme majesty, having accomplished what is to be done, Maheśvara, // 14
unborn, self-manifest, the twenty-sixth, unchanging, unmoving, and constant.
From him the principles are born, and the puruṣa together with the guṇas; // 15
and into him alone they dissolve, in the twenty-sixth, Maheśvara.
Having known this Maheśāna, the perfection of liberation is attained. // 16

Knowing this, one would not be stained by actions which are bonds of delusion.
Just as fire at the end burns the multitude of beings without remainder, // 17
so one who knows the category of the twenty-sixth burns away actions.
Just as all-pervading space is subtle and not stained at all, // 18
so the yogin devoted to the twenty-sixth is not stained by sins.

all [beings] beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the aggregate of beings without remainder. // 20

[All] arises from Īśvara, O Vyāsa, and dissolves back into him alone. / There is indeed nothing other beyond him; one should know him as omnipresent. (21)
He whom the perfected, knowers of the inner self, worship as the Supreme Self, / is this all-pervading god, the twenty-sixth [principle], the supreme Lord. (22)
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna— / the five vital airs in the body—one should strive to restrain them. (23) / Having attentively unified apāna and samāna, / one should place prāṇa along with vyāna into udāna. (24)
By the power of yoga one should bring the breath once to the tip of the nose; / adopting a propitious gaze, one should then contemplate the twenty-sixth [principle]. (25) / Fifteen mātrās are declared to be the first fixing of the joints; / twenty mātrās are to be known as the fifth division of the joints. (26) / In a noiseless, solitary place, free from desire and with senses conquered, / [assuming] svastika, padma, bhadra, or siṃha or kūrma, (27)

7.18.m:
Merely by the taking up of ashes, all bonds are untied for them. / Merely upon being touched with the ash purified by mantras, one is freed. / Fire consumes what is made by Soma, and they know Īśvara to be fire; / fire, united with Soma again, burns what is done and undone. / All the proud ones, headed by Brahmā, were liberated by ashes; / the ash is the power of his splendour; the ash is Īśvara, the purifier.
He who bathes with ashes redeems himself, O Vyāsa; / by ashes and Śiva-yoga, he is freed from the bondage of the snare.
The gods arise from Soma; the ancestors originate from fire. / Therefore, the entire universe, consisting of fire and Soma, is established. / Īśvara is both fire and Soma; ash is said to be that splendour. / Touched by his splendour, twice-born one, one is freed from birth.
Abandoning Sāṃkhya, sciences, austerity, and Vedic rites, / purified solely by bathing in ashes, one goes to that state. . . 8.180.20 . .

7.18.m:
Nothing whatsoever manifested existing in the universe; / the pure, spotless, imperishable, supreme divine shone. . . 8.180.30 . .
Beyond all states of existence and qualities, without conceptual differentiation, unblemished, / moving outside and inside, radiant, imperishable, excellent, and constant; / listen as that imperishable Brahman is declared: / in the beginning, the single syllable 'Om' [arose], from which the perishable emerged; / having three phonemes and three morae, the syllable Om is proclaimed as Brahman. . . 32 . .
In the syllable 'A' is Viṣṇu, but in 'U' is the Grandfather [Brahmā]; / in 'M' is the Lord Īśa; in the subtle measure (mātrā), Prakṛti is traditionally taught.
Those two gods who are known as Brahmā and Viṣṇu came forth from Īśvara; / assuming female form, Prakṛti constantly stays beside the Lord.

7.18.m:
In the form of a wife, she, Prakṛti, constantly worships Śambhu. / Prakṛti is indeed known as the perishable (kṣara), while Īśvara himself is the imperishable (akṣara).
For she, Prakṛti, who binds through the guṇas, came forth from Īśvara; / Mahādeva is her creator, from whom Viṣṇu and the Grandfather arose
as the two lords of creatures bound by the three guṇas. / Pervading those two who abide in Prakṛti and consist of the guṇas, Maheśa,
abiding in the syllable 'M', having become the omnipresent lord, experiences and moves about. / Having understood this supreme secret, the imperishable reality has been spoken by me.
By whichever meditating sage, O Vyāsa, this Īśvara is conceptualized, / that sage, having entered him, becomes liberated in soul and fulfilled.
Those who are not on the true path, dedicated [only] to logic and inference, do not know him, / the enjoyer of Prakṛti, the supreme Lord designated as the twenty-sixth [principle].
Oṃkāra is Prakṛti eternally, and within it Īśvara is situated, / just as ghee is situated within milk, O Vyāsa.
By one who meditates on Oṃkāra, having transcended Prakṛti, O sage, / and has known that great Īśvara, he is freed from the bonds of beasts (paśu).
Prakṛti is called Īśvarī; she causes delusion through the bondage of the guṇas. / Due to the nature of Brahman she expands, and due to the nature of Viṣṇu she resorts to pervasive power.
By the grace of Īśvara, this Prakṛti, consisting of the three guṇas, / possessed of ego, is the creator of the world; Maheśvara is her enjoyer.
Eight-armed and three-footed, she has five bodies and faces; / two-eyed, engaged in the five actions, mounted on a chariot drawn by seven horses,

7.18.m:
Arising, destruction, the performance of rites, / the instrumental cause, origin, and womb—these are, in brief, her states.
Oṃkāra was born from Īśvara, and it is established in him; / from Oṃkāra everything was born, the universe up to the realm of Brahmā.
Therefore, O fortunate one, yogins such as Kapila / worship Oṃkāra as the supreme, unconditioned Brahman.
He alone is the all-pervading Self, and he alone is the cause. / Thus, knowing Viṣṇu and the Grandfather, who have become Prakṛti and originate from Oṃkāra,
as the objects of enjoyment for the Lord and consisting of the guṇas, / abandoning their creations known as the Vedas and sacrifices which bind through ritual duty,
which are great delusions grounded in darkness (tamas), connected with attachment to sense-objects, / preceded by clarity (sattva), centered in passion (rajas), and ever accompanied by pleasure and pain,
wandering in worldly existence, deluded, and endowed with all that is impermanent— / the wise man, devoted to the yoga of meditation, should yearn for Īśvara.
From him Prakṛti arose, and into him alone she dissolves. / He by whom that Īśvara is known, established in the Self through yoga— / Prakṛti does not bind him, and he is liberated from the ocean of worldly existence.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-seventh chapter on the rule of meditation in the description of Pāśupata yoga in the Skandapurāṇa.

Another channel is called Suṣumṇā, situated in soma, fire, and the mind. / In this body endowed with elements, it is situated in the Kūrmāra wind,
attached to the ankle and the palm of the hand, contracting and extending. / Joined with the Samāna and Vyāna [winds], it satisfies blood and flesh.
The other wind which is Udāna and that which is called Kūrmāra, / both of those are established in balance in the channel tied to the navel.
One wind moves downward through the channel, and the other moves upward from it. / The one staying below is connected to the feet; the one going upward is situated in the head.
The wind named Devadatta and the other wind Kṛtaka, / both are tied to fire and soma, the very strong causes of the vital breath.
One increases the fire, and the other satisfies the soma. / Devadatta, Mahānāga, Kṛta, Kūrma, and Dhanañjaya—
these are well-known as the five vital breaths, the fires of the sacrificer. / Whatever is offered or sacrificed into these approaches the soma.

And that is proclaimed as the immortal nectar; it is declared to be attainable through knowledge.
There is no higher goal of knowledge and discernment than that. (51)
Having understood this thus, one should abandon delusion born from the transformation of the three qualities.
Of that indivisible Self, the twenty-sixth [principle], the Lord, (52)
who else adept in yoga would make a division from the Blessed Lord?
One should not imagine diversity in that spotless, indeterminate master. (53)
Free from delusion, with associations abandoned, devoid of actions and duties,
those who observe the vow of the Lord enter into that great Lord. (54)
Thus this Māheśvara yoga has been declared to you, Vyāsa,
which is the correct union with the Lord, such as is found nowhere else. (55)
Whatever doubt you have, O brahmin, and whatever you consider should be asked,
ask that at once, O holy one; I have nothing that cannot be told to you. (56)
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter in the Skandapurāṇa, in the description of Pāśupata yoga, on the rules of yoga.

Vyāsa said:
O blessed Lord, ruler of all yogins, bowed to by all immortals,
oh, the knowledge dispelling ignorance has been spoken by you! (1)
Today my doubts regarding Mahādeva, the Supreme, are gone.
Prakṛti was born from Śaṅkara; Brahmā and Viṣṇu have that nature. (2)

Having first spoken the entire saṃhitā concerning every path of yoga, (3)
who else speaks in this manner of knowledge, both partless and with parts?
From hearing this, O chief of brahmins, I have understood the body to be released. (4)

Therefore I ask this of you; you ought to declare the final state.
Having thus become endowed with discernment, the sage who has attained yoga, O sage, (6)

attain that partless Brahman, the supreme Lord? (7)
Tell me, O best of sages, the means to achieve fixation on the Lord, which yields liberation;
I have nothing else to ask. (8)
Addressed thus by his disciple, the very noble Vyāsa,
the chief of brahmins declared the certainty of the Śiva doctrine. (9)
Sanatkumāra said:
Listen, Vyāsa, to the supreme knowledge, the cause of fixation on the Lord,
by which yogins intent on knowledge are liberated at their own will. (10)
Having understood this three-fold departure and practicing it repeatedly indeed,
abandoning one's own body like an enemy, one should attain absorption in the twenty-sixth [principle]. (11)

The wind named Dhanañjaya, which always throbs in the heart—

drawn back into the navel, the triad is detached in the pericarp. (24)

7.18.m:
[Death occurring] through contact with poison, weapons, or fire, or through snakes, fanged beasts, diseases, or water, / is renowned as external death; now learn from me concerning bodily [death]. // 28
Internal death may be born of disease or born of time. / Born of time is said to be through old age, while born of disease is from the destruction [of the body] by ailment. // 29
This other death, O sage, is difficult to attain: that which arises from uniting in yoga; / that which is brought about by the means of yoga, and that which comes from the expiration of time. // 30
Listen in brief, O Vyāsa, to the difference and change between the two: / one occurs from the expiration of time, whereas the second is desired by the mind. // 31
This sound born of ringing which is heard joined in the ear, / that merges first into Kūrma; by that, fire abandons its luster. // 32
Then, bereft of luster, that fire is separated from conjunction with sound; / surpassing the qualities of sound and touch, it abandons its connection to form. // 33
When fire has thus perished, all the vital winds then, / desiring union in one place, tear through the vital points. // 34

7.18.m:
Kūrmāra, Devadatta, Kṛkara, and Nāga indeed, / quickly joining with Udāna, enter into the pericarp [of the heart]. // 35
Then the breath ascends upward, [bringing] the departure of mind and individual self; / then whatever light was in the two eyes quickly enters the moon. // 36
The senses go into the mind, and the mind into the departure of prāṇa; / when all of them have dissolved, the wind oppresses the vital breaths. // 37
Then, being oppressed, all those winds become unified, / each having abandoned its own location, activity, and essential nature. // 38
All the winds situated together fill Dhanañjaya; / remaining there indeed, Kūrmāra stays, having abandoned the individual self. // 39
